name: Subcision / TCA CROSS

lead: Subcision releases depressed acne scars so the skin surface looks smoother. TCA CROSS is a separate acid-based procedure often mentioned alongside it for scars.

A needle under the skin cuts the fibrous bands holding a scar down, letting it rise, and the wound-healing response adds collagen. Subcision was described in 1995, and dermatology reviews treat it as one part of combined scar care, supported by small case series and registered trials.

paras: Clinicians use it mainly on rolling acne scars, often when other treatments have not lifted tethered scars. It is commonly combined with other scar treatments, and improvement develops over weeks as healing proceeds. Forum accounts of self-performed versions exist, but it is a clinic procedure.

Bleeding, bruising and infection are possible, and clinical guidance lists bleeding disorders, infection and keloid tendency as reasons to avoid it. Limited complication data were found in the sources reviewed.

chain: Depressed scar lifts and collagen forms
angle.text: Subcision cuts the fibres tethering rolling acne scars so the depressed skin lifts and new collagen forms, giving a smoother surface. TCA CROSS is a related acid-based scar technique, and small studies and reviews describe subcision as part of combined care.

lead: Subcision is a minor in-office procedure for depressed (atrophic) scars in which a needle or blunt cannula is passed beneath the skin to cut the fibrous bands that hold a scar down, so the surface can rise toward the level of the surrounding skin. It was named and described in 1995 by Orentreich and Orentreich as subcutaneous incisionless surgery for depressed scars and wrinkles.[1] People use it to even out the contour of rolling acne scars, the shadowed, wave-like depressions that make skin look uneven under side lighting.[2][3]

TCA CROSS (chemical reconstruction of skin scars) is a separate scar procedure in which a high concentration of trichloroacetic acid is applied in small amounts to the base of narrow, deep scars, mainly icepick scars, to prompt the skin to rebuild collagen from within the scar. It is grouped with subcision in scar-treatment discussion because the two address different scar types and are often combined in multimodality plans.[4][5][6]

Subcision has also been studied for cellulite, and a series of small randomized and split-face trials has examined it alone and combined with suction, radiofrequency, platelet-rich plasma, stromal-vascular fraction cells, exosomes and lasers.[7][8][9][10][11][12] On looksmax.org, subcision is discussed as a step for tethered scars that other treatments have not changed, and the forum includes self-performed accounts; this article records that the practice is discussed and does not describe how to perform it.[13][14]
infobox: Minor in-office procedure (subcision); chemical scar procedure (TCA CROSS)

Dermatology or aesthetic clinic, local anaesthesia

paras: In the original description, a tri-beveled hypodermic needle is introduced through a skin puncture, hence incisionless, and its sharp edges are moved under the defect to make cuts beneath the skin surface. The authors reported that releasing the tethered tissue raises the depression and that connective tissue formed during normal wound healing adds to the lift.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, adds that blunt cannulas of roughly 18 to 21 gauge are also used, that sessions are done under local anaesthesia and take roughly half an hour to an hour, and that bruising, swelling and tenderness typically settle in a week or two.[15] Practitioner descriptions say the procedure works best on tethered, rolling scars; Grokipedia lists bleeding disorders, active infection and a tendency to form keloids as contraindications.[15]

Variants described in the literature include suction-assisted subcision, cannula-based subcision, subcision combined with fillers or injected growth-factor preparations, and energy-based versions such as endo-radiofrequency subcision, in which a radiofrequency probe delivers heat under the scar.[15][16][10][12]

A widely cited 2001 classification by Jacob, Dover and Kaminer divides atrophic acne scars into icepick, boxcar and rolling types, with treatment choice depending on type; its treatment algorithm lists punch excision, punch elevation, subcision and laser resurfacing among the options.[2] A 2019 update reviewed newer and developing options within that system.[3] Reviews of multimodality care note that subcision is often combined with lasers, peels, fillers or microneedling, and that scar type guides the choice.[4][5] A 2011 report described combined microneedling and glycolic acid peels for acne scars in dark skin, listing subcision among the options for scars.[17]

TCA CROSS was reported in 2008 by Fabbrocini and colleagues, who applied 50% trichloroacetic acid to atrophic acne or chickenpox scars in five patients at 4-week intervals for three sessions; they reported cosmetic improvement in depth and appearance, and noted that the lower concentration than the 90% used in earlier work was chosen to limit local adverse effects.[6] A 2025 randomized trial of 40 patients compared 70% and 100% TCA used with the CROSS technique; patient and researcher scores did not differ significantly, the 100% group showed greater efficacy on icepick than boxcar scars, and crusting lasted significantly longer with 100%.[18] A 2023 evidence review lists trichloroacetic acid peels among treatments with stronger supporting evidence for atrophic acne scars.[19]

In a 2005 case series, Alam, Omura and Kaminer treated 40 patients with rolling acne scars using a standardised subcision technique. At six months, patients and investigators each reported roughly 50 percent improvement and about 90 percent of patients said their appearance had improved; swelling, bruising and pain were described as transient, and some patients had persistent firm bumps at the treatment site.[20]

A 2024 split-face randomized, evaluator-blinded trial in five patients with rolling scars gave one side five subcision sessions four weeks apart and left the other untreated. Global scarring scores fell more on the treated side by week 36, and half of the patients were more satisfied with the treated side.[9] A 2024 split-face trial of subcision with or without suction found no difference between arms in blinded dermatologist ratings at one or four months, while subjects rated improvement higher with suction at one month (37 percent versus 24 percent) but not at four months.[10] A 2022 double-blind trial in 10 patients found that adding stromal-vascular fraction cells to subcision produced larger changes in measured scar volume and area at three months than subcision alone, with no complications reported.[11] A 2023 pilot trial of endo-radiofrequency subcision in 30 patients reported a fall in mean Goodman and Baron score from 13.2 to 5.4 and describes side effects as minimal and transient.[12]

Reviews describe the evidence base as limited by small trials and varied scoring. A 2016 and a 2019 review note few high-quality comparisons and call subcision one of several surgical options; a 2023 review places it among treatments with lesser-quality evidence than lasers, microneedling, platelet-rich plasma and chemical peels, and a 2024 narrative review says no treatment is yet a gold standard and that combinations are likely to give more benefit.[3][4][19][21] Grokipedia cites a review of 16 trials that reported larger average improvement with blunt cannulas than needles, a figure that has not been independently checked here.[15]

Registered trials include subcision with CO2 laser or PRP versus subcision alone (42 participants, 2025) [22]; subcision with injected exosomes versus subcision alone (20 participants, 2024, completed) [23]; subcision with suction (20 participants, 2012, completed) [24]; multiple subcisions on rolling scars (5 participants, 2014) [25]; cannula versus needle subcision for post-traumatic atrophic facial scars (50 participants, 2021) [16]; and combination procedures for acne scarring (30 participants, 2007) [26]. Laser treatments for facial acne scars have been reviewed separately.[27]

Hexsel and Mazzuco reported subcision for cellulite in a series of 232 women aged 18 to 52 treated between January 1995 and January 1998 for thigh and buttock cellulite, describing it as useful for advanced-grade cellulite.[7] A 2017 review focused on subcision in cellulite, and cellulite trials combining subcision with cryolipolysis are registered.[8][28] Cellulite reviews describe a wide set of options including lasers, radiofrequency and acoustic-wave therapy alongside subcision, and note that treatment remains challenging.[8]

Reported effects in the case series were transient swelling, bruising and pain, with some persistent firm nodules.[20] Grokipedia lists bruising, swelling, pinpoint bleeding and temporary redness as common, hematoma and post-procedure hyperpigmentation (more likely in darker skin) as possible, and infection or nerve injury as less common, and says sharp cannulas are associated with more events than blunt ones.[15] TCA CROSS trials report burning during treatment, frosting and crusting, with longer crusting at 100% concentration.[18] Complication data across trials are limited by small sizes.[9]

A looksmax.org thread promotes subcision as a procedure that releases scars from underlying tissue and can be followed by lasers or peels.[13] Another thread presents a long self-performed (DIY) guide for atrophic acne scars; this article does not reproduce its method.[14] A T Nation post mentions a dermatology office where TCA CROSS, laser treatments, dermarolling and excisions were seen for scarring and collagen production.[29]

timeline.event: Orentreich and Orentreich describe and name subcision.[1]
Hexsel and Mazzuco begin treating cellulite with subcision; the 232-patient series covers 1995 to 1998 (published 2000).[7]
Jacob, Dover and Kaminer propose the icepick, boxcar and rolling acne scar classification.[2]
Alam, Omura and Kaminer publish a 40-patient report on subcision technique and outcomes.[20]
Fabbrocini and colleagues describe the CROSS technique with 50% TCA in five patients.[6]
A trial of subcision with suction on acne scars begins.[24]
A review of cellulite with a focus on subcision is published.[8]
A review updates acne scar treatment options within the classification system.[3]
Pilot trial of endo-radiofrequency subcision in 30 patients; evidence review of atrophic acne scarring published.[12][19]
Split-face randomized trials of multiple subcisions and of subcision with suction are published.[9][10]
Randomized comparison of 70% versus 100% TCA CROSS is published.[18]
